T3-1519.ex: 그 사람은 나이를 속이고 회사에 들어갔어요.
T3-1519.x: That person lied about their age to get into the company.

T3-1520.ex: 엄마는 제 기분이 안 좋은 것을 바로 알아차렸어요.
T3-1520.x: My mom noticed right away that I was in a bad mood.

T3-1521.ex: 그 선수는 움직임이 아주 빠르고 가벼워요.
T3-1521.x: That player's movements are very quick and light.
T3-1521.e: 움직이다 'to move' + -ㅁ, which turns verbs into nouns.

T3-1522.forms: 이끌어요 · 이끌었어요 · 이끌 거예요 · 이끄세요 (ㄹ drops)
T3-1522.x: Coach Kim led the team to the championship.
T3-1522.e: 끌다 'to pull' with a leading 이- — pulling others along.

T3-1523.m: to continue, go on; to be connected, lead to
T3-1523.x: The meeting went on until late at night.
T3-1523.t: Also 'lead to': 작은 실수가 큰 사고로 이어질 수 있어요 'a small mistake can lead to an accident.'

T3-1524.m: to cause, bring about; to raise, help (someone) up
T3-1524.ex: 담배는 여러 가지 병을 일으킬 수 있어요.
T3-1524.e: Causative partner of 일어나다 'to get up, happen'.

T3-1525.forms: 이어요 · 이었어요 · 이을 거예요 · 이으세요 (ㅅ irregular)
T3-1525.m: to connect, join; to carry on, succeed
T3-1525.ex: 이 다리는 섬과 육지를 잇고 있어요.
T3-1525.x: This bridge connects the island to the mainland.
T3-1525.t: The ㅅ drops before vowels: 잇다 → 이어요, and 가업을 잇다 means 'to take over the family business.'

T3-1526.m: to take up, occupy; to account for; to win (a place)
T3-1526.ex: 이 큰 침대가 방의 반을 차지해요.
T3-1526.x: This big bed takes up half the room.

T3-1527.m: to spread, get around; to become soggy (noodles)
T3-1527.ex: 그 소문이 학교 전체에 금방 퍼졌어요.
T3-1527.x: That rumor quickly spread throughout the whole school.
T3-1527.t: Koreans also say 라면이 퍼졌어요 when instant noodles have sat too long and gone soggy.

T3-1528.m: to head for, go toward; to face
T3-1528.x: We headed for Busan early in the morning.
T3-1528.e: From a syllable meaning 'direction, toward', as in 방향 'direction'.
T3-1528.t: N을/를 향해 means 'toward N': 꿈을 향해 'toward one's dream'.

T3-1529.m: to grow, tend (plants, a garden); to take care of (one's looks)
T3-1529.x: My grandmother grows flowers and vegetables in the yard.

T3-1530.m: to break off, snap; to bend, turn; to defeat
T3-1530.x: You're not allowed to pick flowers in the park.

T3-1531.m: to step forward, come forward; to set out, leave
T3-1531.ex: 아무도 하지 않아서 제가 먼저 나섰어요.
T3-1531.x: Nobody would do it, so I stepped up first.

T3-1532.m: to put out, take out; to present, release; to offer
T3-1532.ex: 그 회사가 올해 새로운 제품을 내놓았어요.
T3-1532.x: That company released a new product this year.
T3-1532.t: Pronounced [내노타]; in speech 내놓아요 often shortens to 내놔요.

T3-1533.ex: 친구들이 제 머리 모양을 보고 놀렸어요.
T3-1533.x: My friends made fun of my hairstyle.
T3-1533.e: Built on 놀다 'to play' — playing at someone's expense.

T3-1534.m: to replace, take the place of, stand in for
T3-1534.ex: 오늘은 제가 김 선생님을 대신해서 수업을 할게요.
T3-1534.x: Today I'll teach the class in place of Mr. Kim.
T3-1534.e: Literally 'replace the body' — standing in for someone.

T3-1535.m: to argue, demand an explanation; to weigh, calculate carefully
T3-1535.ex: 가게에 가서 왜 환불이 안 되는지 따졌어요.
T3-1535.x: I went to the store and demanded to know why I couldn't get a refund.
T3-1535.t: 따져 보다 means 'to think it over carefully': 장단점을 따져 보세요 'weigh the pros and cons.'

T3-1536.x: I messed up an important exam because of a cold.
T3-1536.e: Probably linked to 망하다 'to go to ruin, go bankrupt'.
T3-1536.t: Everyday collocations: 시험을 망치다 'bomb a test', 분위기를 망치다 'kill the mood'.

T3-1537.x: An old building collapsed in the earthquake.

T3-1538.m: to start, launch, hold (an event); to spread out
T3-1538.ex: 시청에서 환경 보호 캠페인을 벌이고 있어요.
T3-1538.x: City Hall is running an environmental protection campaign.
T3-1538.t: Don't mix it up with 벌리다 'to open wide': 입을 벌리다 'open your mouth'.

T3-1539.x: The child broke his toy and is crying.
T3-1539.t: 부수다 is doing the breaking; 부서지다 means something gets broken.

T3-1540.forms: 빌어요 · 빌었어요 · 빌 거예요 · 비세요 (ㄹ drops)
T3-1540.m: to wish, pray; to beg (for forgiveness)
T3-1540.ex: 생일 케이크 앞에서 눈을 감고 소원을 빌었어요.
T3-1540.x: I closed my eyes in front of my birthday cake and made a wish.
T3-1540.t: Don't confuse it with 빌리다 'to borrow'; 행운을 빌어요 means 'good luck'.

T3-1541.m: to swallow; to hold back (tears, words)
T3-1541.ex: 이 약은 씹지 말고 물과 함께 삼키세요.
T3-1541.x: Don't chew this medicine; swallow it with water.

T3-1542.ex: 이미 끝난 일이라서 지금 후회해도 소용없어요.
T3-1542.x: It's already over, so there's no use regretting it now.
T3-1542.e: 소용 'use' + 없다 'not exist' — literally 'there's no use'.
T3-1542.t: Pronounced [소용업따]; common pattern -아/어 봤자 소용없다 'it's no use even if you try.'

T3-1543.m: to spill, pour out; to devote (effort, energy)
T3-1543.x: I accidentally spilled coffee on my laptop.

T3-1544.m: to have (an event) ahead, be just before
T3-1544.ex: 결혼을 앞두고 요즘 준비할 게 많아요.
T3-1544.x: With my wedding coming up, I have a lot to prepare these days.
T3-1544.e: 앞 'front' + 두다 'to put' — something placed just ahead of you.
T3-1544.t: Almost always used as N을/를 앞두고 'with N just ahead': 시험을 앞두고.

T3-1545.forms: 애써요 · 애썼어요 · 애쓸 거예요 · 애쓰세요 (ㅡ drops)
T3-1545.m: to try hard, make an effort, strive
T3-1545.ex: 모두 이번 행사를 위해 애써 주셔서 감사합니다.
T3-1545.x: Thank you all for working so hard on this event.
T3-1545.t: 애쓰셨어요 is a warm way to thank someone for their effort.

T3-1546.m: to go against, violate; to be out of line; to miss each other
T3-1546.x: That kind of behavior goes against school rules.
T3-1546.t: Pronounced [어근나다] — nasalization; common as 규칙에 어긋나다 'break the rules'.

T3-1547.x: The crowd shouted the player's name loudly.

T3-1548.m: to ring, sound; to make (someone) cry
T3-1548.x: A phone suddenly rang in the middle of class.
T3-1548.e: Causative of 울다 'to cry', which also covers bells and birds 'crying'.
T3-1548.t: Two senses: 벨이 울리다 'a bell rings' and 아이를 울리다 'make a child cry'.

T3-1549.m: to depend on, rely on, lean on
T3-1549.x: I relied on my family a lot when things were hard.
T3-1549.t: Homonym warning: the noun 의지 also means 'willpower', a different word.

T3-1550.m: to be locked; to be submerged; to be lost (in thought)
T3-1550.ex: 문이 잠겨서 집에 들어갈 수 없어요.
T3-1550.x: The door is locked, so I can't get into the house.
T3-1550.e: Passive of 잠그다 'to lock'; a homonym means 'to be submerged'.
T3-1550.t: Also 목이 잠기다 'to lose one's voice' and 생각에 잠기다 'to be lost in thought'.

T3-1551.forms: 질러요 · 질렀어요 · 지를 거예요 · 지르세요 (르 irregular)
T3-1551.m: to yell, scream (with 소리); to kick; to set (fire)
T3-1551.x: I screamed while watching a scary movie.
T3-1551.t: Learn it in chunks: 소리를 지르다 'scream', 불을 지르다 'set a fire'.

T3-1552.ex: 옆이 너무 시끄러워서 공부에 집중이 안 돼요.
T3-1552.x: It's so noisy next to me that I can't focus on studying.
T3-1552.t: Pronounced [집쭝]; 집중이 안 되다 is the natural way to say 'I can't concentrate.'

T3-1553.m: to chase, pursue; to drive away
T3-1553.x: The cat is running around the yard chasing a mouse.

T3-1554.ex: 너무 화가 나서 편지를 찢어 버렸어요.
T3-1554.x: I was so angry that I tore up the letter.

T3-1555.m: to find out, discover, track down
T3-1555.x: The police tracked down the lost wallet.
T3-1555.e: 찾다 'to look for' + -아 내다 'manage to, all the way'.

T3-1556.forms: 치러요 · 치렀어요 · 치를 거예요 · 치르세요 (ㅡ drops)
T3-1556.m: to take (an exam); to hold (a ceremony); to pay
T3-1556.x: I take my final exams next week.
T3-1556.t: A common mistake: the past tense is 치렀어요, not 치뤘어요.

T3-1557.m: to splash, spatter; to bounce; to stand out
T3-1557.x: A car went by and muddy water splashed on my clothes.

T3-1558.m: to dig; to carve; to dig into (study deeply)
T3-1558.x: The kids are digging in the sand at the beach and playing.
T3-1558.t: Watch out: 팔 거예요 and 파세요 look the same as forms of 팔다 'to sell'; context decides.

T3-1559.ex: 학생이 적어서 두 반을 합쳐서 수업했어요.
T3-1559.x: There weren't many students, so we combined the two classes.

T3-1560.m: to accomplish, pull off, manage to do
T3-1560.x: It was really hard, but we finally pulled it off.
T3-1560.e: 하다 'to do' + -아 내다 'see it through to the end'.
T3-1560.t: 해냈다! is the classic shout of 'I did it!'

T3-1561.m: to wander, to roam; to be lost, to struggle to find
T3-1561.ex: 길을 몰라서 한 시간 동안 헤맸어요.
T3-1561.x: I didn't know the way, so I wandered around for an hour.
T3-1561.e: Picture someone going in circles; also used for struggling with a problem.

T3-1562.e: Homonym warning: also 'to wipe quickly', as in 눈물을 훔치다 (wipe away tears).
T3-1562.t: 훔쳐 가다 (steal and take away) is the most natural way to say something got stolen.

T3-1563.ex: 해가 뜨기 전 새벽의 바다는 아주 고요했어요.
T3-1563.x: Before sunrise, the sea at dawn was very still.
T3-1563.e: More poetic than 조용하다; often describes nature, nights, and atmospheres.

T3-1564.x: This painting is a truly precious work.
T3-1564.e: Literally 'precious, honored'; 귀하 is also a formal 'you' in letters.
T3-1564.t: 귀한 손님 (an honored guest) is a common polite collocation.

T3-1565.ex: 이 칼은 아주 날카로우니까 조심해서 쓰세요.
T3-1565.x: This knife is very sharp, so use it carefully.
T3-1565.e: From 날 (blade) + -카롭다; used for knives, eyes, remarks, and moods.
T3-1565.t: Also used for people: 날카로운 질문 (a sharp question) or 신경이 날카롭다 (to be on edge).

T3-1566.ex: 한국은 봄, 여름, 가을, 겨울이 뚜렷한 나라예요.
T3-1566.x: Korea is a country with distinct spring, summer, fall, and winter seasons.
T3-1566.t: Pronounced [뚜려타다] — the final ㅅ and ㅎ merge into ㅌ.

T3-1567.x: There's no good place to eat lunch.
T3-1567.e: Often negative: 마땅한 게 없다 means 'nothing quite suitable'.

T3-1568.m: intact, fine, in perfect condition; sound, sane
T3-1568.x: I fell on the street, but luckily my phone is fine.

T3-1569.x: That movie's ending was way too predictable.
T3-1569.e: Don't confuse with -ㄹ 뻔하다 'almost did': 넘어질 뻔했어요 = I almost fell.
T3-1569.t: -ㄹ 게 뻔하다 means 'it's obvious that...', e.g. 늦을 게 뻔해요 (he's obviously going to be late).

T3-1570.ex: 그 디자이너는 아주 섬세한 작품을 만들어요.
T3-1570.x: That designer makes very delicate work.
T3-1570.e: Literally 'fine and thin', like delicate threads.

T3-1571.ex: 호텔에서는 귀중한 물건을 프런트에 맡기는 게 좋아요.
T3-1571.x: At a hotel, it's best to leave valuable items at the front desk.

T3-1572.x: These things are useless now, so I'll throw them away.
T3-1572.e: 쓸모 (use, usefulness, from 쓰다 'to use') + 없다 'not have'.
T3-1572.t: Pronounced [쓸모업따]; the modifier is 쓸모없는, not 쓸모없은.

T3-1573.ex: 어제 콘서트에 엄청난 수의 사람들이 모여서 깜짝 놀랐어요.
T3-1573.x: I was shocked that an enormous crowd gathered at the concert yesterday.
T3-1573.e: The adverb 엄청 (super, really) is hugely common in casual speech.

T3-1574.x: King Sejong is the great king who created Hangeul.
T3-1574.e: Literally 'grand and big'; reserved for historic figures and achievements.
T3-1574.t: Much stronger than English 'great'; for 'a great meal' use 훌륭하다 or 최고, not 위대하다.

T3-1575.ex: 외국어를 잘하면 취업할 때 아주 유리해요.
T3-1575.x: Being good at a foreign language is a big advantage when job hunting.
T3-1575.t: Pattern: N에 유리하다 (favorable for N). Don't confuse with 유리 'glass', a different word.

T3-1576.ex: 비가 와서 우리 팀에 불리한 경기였어요.
T3-1576.x: It rained, so the game was unfavorable for our team.

T3-1577.ex: 오늘 들은 강의는 정말 재미있고 유익했어요.
T3-1577.x: The lecture I heard today was really fun and informative.
T3-1577.t: Pronounced [유이카다]; 유익한 시간 (a worthwhile time) is a common polite compliment.

T3-1578.m: excessive, too much, over the top
T3-1578.x: Too much exercise is actually bad for your health.
T3-1578.e: From 지나다 'to pass'; going past the line. As a verb, it means 'to pass by'.
T3-1578.t: 지나치게 + adjective (지나치게 비싸요) is a formal way to say 'too'.

T3-1579.x: I'm not joking; I'm saying this seriously.
T3-1579.t: Describes attitude, not severity: a 'serious illness' is 심각한 병, not 진지한 병.

T3-1580.x: You have to prepare thoroughly before the exam.

T3-1581.ex: 이 노래는 한국 사람들에게 아주 친숙해요.
T3-1581.x: This song is very familiar to Koreans.
T3-1581.t: 친숙하다 = familiar to people (N에게 친숙하다); 익숙하다 = being used to something yourself.

T3-1582.x: That café's interior is really unusual.

T3-1583.ex: 아침 일찍 가 보면 시장은 언제나 활기차요.
T3-1583.x: If you go early in the morning, the market is always lively.
T3-1583.e: 활기 'lively energy' + native 차다 'to be full': full of life.

T3-1584.x: That person's fingers are long and slender.
T3-1584.e: For thin long things (threads, fingers); flat thin things use 얇다.
T3-1584.t: The modifier 가는 looks like 가는 from 가다 'going'; context tells you which.

T3-1585.x: Suddenly big raindrops started to fall.
T3-1585.e: For cylinder-like thickness (arms, rope); thick books use 두껍다.
T3-1585.t: Pronounced [국따]; before a vowel the ㄹ comes back: 굵어요 [굴거요].

T3-1586.x: In winter the air is dry, so my hands get rough.
T3-1586.e: Covers rough textures, rough waves, and rough or rude speech.

T3-1587.x: The surface of this desk is very smooth.
T3-1587.e: Used for surfaces and also for smooth speech or writing.
T3-1587.t: Don't mix up with 미끄럽다 (slippery, e.g. icy roads); 매끄럽다 is a pleasant smoothness.

T3-1588.x: This meat is very tender and delicious.
T3-1588.e: Literally 'soft'; for food, colors, and coffee strength alike.
T3-1588.t: 연한 커피 = weak coffee, 연한 파란색 = light blue; the opposite is 진하다.

T3-1589.ex: 한국의 여름은 비가 많이 오고 아주 무더워요.
T3-1589.x: Summer in Korea is rainy and very hot and humid.
T3-1589.e: Probably from 물 'water' + 덥다 'hot': wet heat.
T3-1589.t: Weather reports say 무더위 (sweltering heat) and 무더운 날씨 for muggy summer days.

T3-1590.x: Even though it's winter, the weather is mild like spring today.
T3-1590.e: Think of a soft blanket: used for bedding, hugs, and mild winter days.

T3-1591.ex: 저는 주말마다 집 근처 마트에서 식료품을 사요.
T3-1591.x: I buy groceries at the supermarket near my house every weekend.
T3-1591.t: Pronounced [싱뇨품] — nasalization turns ㄱ+ㄹ into ㅇ+ㄴ.

T3-1592.ex: 고추장을 넣고 밥을 잘 비벼 드세요.
T3-1592.x: Add the red pepper paste and mix the rice well before eating.
T3-1592.e: The root of 비빔밥 'mixed rice' and 비빔국수 'mixed noodles'.

T3-1593.forms: 저어요 · 저었어요 · 저을 거예요 · 저으세요 (ㅅ irregular)
T3-1593.m: to stir; to row (a boat); to shake (one's head)
T3-1593.x: Stir slowly until the sugar dissolves.
T3-1593.e: Same stirring motion in 노를 젓다 'row' and 고개를 젓다 'shake one's head no'.
T3-1593.t: The ㅅ drops before vowels: 저어요, not 젓어요.

T3-1594.forms: 담가요 · 담갔어요 · 담글 거예요 · 담그세요 (ㅡ drops)
T3-1594.m: to make (kimchi, pickles), to pickle; to soak, to dip
T3-1594.x: Grandma makes kimjang kimchi every year.
T3-1594.e: Basic idea: putting something into liquid — soaking, or brining kimchi.
T3-1594.t: Standard forms are 담가요 and 담갔어요; 담궈요 is a very common mistake, even among natives.

T3-1595.ex: 요즘 유기농 채소를 찾는 사람이 많아요.
T3-1595.x: These days many people look for organic vegetables.

T3-1596.ex: 밤에 배가 고파서 야식으로 치킨을 시켰어요.
T3-1596.x: I got hungry at night, so I ordered fried chicken as a late-night snack.
T3-1596.e: Literally 'night food' — a big part of Korean delivery culture.

T3-1597.x: He indirectly let me know he was saying no.
T3-1597.e: Literally 'touching through something in between'. -적 = '-ic, -al': 경제적, 문화적.

T3-1598.x: Stress has a direct effect on your health.
T3-1598.t: 직접 alone usually means 'in person, oneself' (직접 만들었어요); 직접적 means 'direct' in a logical sense.

T3-1599.forms: 갈수록 + 더/점점: 날이 갈수록 · 시간이 갈수록
T3-1599.m: increasingly, more and more as time goes on
T3-1599.ex: 시간이 갈수록 한국어 공부가 더 재미있어져요.
T3-1599.x: As time goes on, studying Korean gets more and more fun.
T3-1599.e: 가다 'to go' + -ㄹ수록 'the more...': 'the further it goes'.
T3-1599.t: Usually paired with -아/어지다: 갈수록 어려워져요 (it keeps getting harder).

T3-1600.x: This concept was hard to understand at first.
T3-1600.t: Slang: 개념 없다 means someone has no common sense or manners.

T3-1601.x: This park is open to citizens even at night.

T3-1602.ex: 자기 자신을 객관적으로 보는 것은 어려워요.
T3-1602.x: It's hard to see yourself objectively.
T3-1602.e: Literally 'a guest's view' — seeing from outside.

T3-1603.x: This is purely my own subjective opinion.
T3-1603.e: Literally 'the host's view' — seeing from inside.

T3-1604.m: to refuse, to reject, to deny
T3-1604.t: 거부하다 is stronger and more formal than 거절하다, which is a polite 'no' to an offer.

T3-1605.x: This river is the boundary between the two cities.
T3-1605.e: Homonym warning: another 경계 means 'caution, alert', as in 경계하다.

T3-1606.x: Traveling broke a lot of my stereotypes.

T3-1607.ex: 경기에서 심판은 항상 공정하게 판단해야 합니다.
T3-1607.x: In a game, the referee must always judge fairly.

T3-1608.x: The broken part needs to be replaced.

T3-1609.ex: 건강하게 살려면 일과 생활의 균형이 중요해요.
T3-1609.x: To live healthily, work-life balance is important.

T3-1610.ex: 그 책을 읽고 큰 깨달음을 얻었어요.
T3-1610.x: I gained a big insight from reading that book.
T3-1610.e: Noun from 깨닫다 'to realize' (ㄷ irregular: 깨달아요).

T3-1611.ex: 그 사람의 말은 논리가 맞지 않아요.
T3-1611.x: What that person says doesn't make logical sense.
T3-1611.t: Pronounced [놀리] — ㄴ before ㄹ becomes ㄹ (liquidization).

T3-1612.x: Try to explain your idea logically.

T3-1613.m: to supplement, to complement, to make up for
T3-1613.x: Make up for the weak parts and resubmit it.

T3-1614.ex: 많은 일을 이제 기계가 대체하고 있어요.
T3-1614.x: Machines are now replacing a lot of jobs.

T3-1615.x: August 15th is the day that celebrates Korea's independence.

T3-1616.m: to become independent; to move out (from parents)
T3-1616.x: I moved out from my parents' place at twenty.

T3-1617.x: My plans after graduation are still vague.

T3-1618.x: That person has a kind side.
T3-1618.e: Literally 'face'. Homonym warning: 면 also means noodles or cotton.
T3-1618.t: Common pattern: -는 면에서 (in terms of), e.g. 가격 면에서 (in terms of price).

T3-1619.x: Please answer the teacher's question clearly.

T3-1620.x: Young people's indifference to politics is a problem.
T3-1620.e: 무 'without' + 관심 'interest'. 무- = 'no, without': 무료, 무책임.

T3-1621.x: My skin is very sensitive to sunlight.
T3-1621.t: Pattern: N에 민감하다 (sensitive to N), used for skin, topics, and prices.

T3-1622.m: to reflect, to incorporate, to take into account
T3-1622.x: We changed the design, incorporating customer feedback.
T3-1622.e: Literally 'to reflect back', like a mirror.

T3-1623.m: to display, to show (ability), to exert
T3-1623.x: That athlete showed his true skill in the final.
T3-1623.e: Literally 'send out and wield' your abilities.

T3-1624.ex: 사고를 방지하기 위해 안전 교육을 합니다.
T3-1624.x: We hold safety training to prevent accidents.

T3-1625.forms: 본래가 · 본래를; also an adverb: 본래 (originally)
T3-1625.ex: 이 카페 건물은 본래 작은 학교였어요.
T3-1625.x: This café building was originally a small school.
T3-1625.t: Pronounced [볼래]; in conversation 원래 is far more common.

T3-1626.x: People's ways of thinking differ a little from country to country.

T3-1627.x: Living costs have gone up a lot due to rising prices.

T3-1628.m: to rise, to go up, to climb
T3-1628.x: Housing prices in Seoul rose sharply this year.
T3-1628.t: News word; in conversation people usually say 오르다: 집값이 올랐어요.

T3-1629.ex: 주가 하락 때문에 걱정하는 사람이 많습니다.
T3-1629.x: Many people are worried because of the drop in stock prices.

T3-1630.m: to fall, to drop, to decline
T3-1630.x: Gas prices have been dropping little by little since yesterday.
T3-1630.t: Pronounced [하라카다]; in conversation people usually say 떨어지다 instead.

T3-1631.x: I try to meet people without preconceptions.

T3-1632.x: My younger sibling has a quiet, introverted disposition.

T3-1633.x: My income went up a little this year compared to last year.

T3-1634.x: You should make important decisions carefully.

T3-1635.ex: 사람의 심리를 이해하는 것은 쉽지 않아요.
T3-1635.t: Pronounced [심니] — ㄹ after ㅁ becomes ㄴ.

T3-1636.x: I feel very anxious mentally before exams.

T3-1637.x: Many people want a stable job.

T3-1638.ex: 이 두 사건은 서로 연관이 있어요.
T3-1638.x: These two incidents are connected to each other.

T3-1639.ex: 그 가수는 젊은 사람들에게 영향력이 커요.
T3-1639.x: That singer has a lot of influence on young people.
T3-1639.e: Literally 'shadow-and-echo power' — the reach you have over others.
T3-1639.t: Pronounced [영향녁]: ㅇ before ㄹ turns ㄹ into ㄴ.

T3-1640.x: There isn't a single exception to this rule.
T3-1640.e: Literally 'outside the examples' — the case that doesn't fit.

T3-1641.x: Stress is a major factor that harms your health.

T3-1642.ex: 바쁠 때는 일의 우선순위를 먼저 정하세요.
T3-1642.x: When you're busy, decide your priorities first.
T3-1642.e: 우선 'first of all' + 순위 'ranking' = ranking of what comes first.

T3-1643.x: The two of them settled the problem amicably.
T3-1643.e: Literally 'round and full' — no sharp edges, nothing missing.
T3-1643.t: Often used as 원만하게 해결하다 'settle amicably' or 대인 관계가 원만하다 'gets along with people'.

T3-1644.ex: 두 회사의 제품은 디자인이 아주 유사해요.
T3-1644.x: The two companies' products are very similar in design.
T3-1644.t: A more formal, written word for 비슷하다; use 비슷하다 in everyday speech.

T3-1645.x: I didn't mean it in a bad way.

T3-1646.m: to depend on, to rely on
T3-1646.x: Kids these days rely too much on their smartphones.
T3-1646.e: Literally 'to exist by leaning on something'.
T3-1646.t: The thing you depend on takes 에: 부모님에게 의존하다, 기계에 의존하다.

T3-1647.x: This house is ideal for a family to live in.
T3-1647.e: 이상 'ideal' + -적 '-like': -적 turns nouns into '-ic/-al' words: 이상적, 현실적.
T3-1647.t: Don't confuse with 이상하다 'strange' — that 이상 is a different word with different hanja.

T3-1648.ex: 이 문제는 일시적인 현상이니까 걱정하지 마세요.
T3-1648.x: This problem is only temporary, so don't worry.
T3-1648.t: Pronounced [일씨적]: ㅅ after ㄹ is tensed.

T3-1649.ex: 학생들이 수업 후에 자발적으로 교실을 청소했어요.
T3-1649.x: The students cleaned the classroom on their own initiative after class.
T3-1649.t: Pronounced [자발쩍]: ㅈ after ㄹ is tensed in -적 words.

T3-1650.x: In the long run, exercise is really necessary.

T3-1651.ex: 큰 목표보다 단기적인 목표부터 세워 보세요.
T3-1651.x: Try setting short-term goals before big ones.

T3-1652.e: Literally 'devoted to one gate' — focused on a single field.

T3-1653.ex: 비자를 받으려면 복잡한 절차를 거쳐야 해요.
T3-1653.x: To get a visa, you have to go through a complicated process.
T3-1653.e: Literally 'sections in order' — the steps done one after another.

T3-1654.x: I'm so busy I can't think straight.
T3-1654.t: 정신이 없다 means 'to be frantic, scatterbrained'; 정신 차려! means 'pull yourself together!'

T3-1655.ex: 일이 많아서 요즘 정신적으로 많이 힘들어요.
T3-1655.x: I've had a lot of work, so I've been struggling mentally lately.

T3-1656.x: This work is very physically demanding.
T3-1656.t: Often paired with its opposite: 정신적으로나 육체적으로 'both mentally and physically'.

T3-1657.ex: 이 방은 색깔의 조화가 정말 좋아요.
T3-1657.x: The colors in this room go together really well.
T3-1657.e: Literally 'tuned into harmony', like instruments playing together.
T3-1657.t: Homonym warning: 조화 can also mean 'artificial flower' (a different word).

T3-1658.ex: 이 마을은 자연과 건물이 조화롭게 어울려요.
T3-1658.x: In this village, the buildings blend harmoniously with nature.

T3-1659.ex: 다음 주에 종합 건강 검진을 받을 거예요.
T3-1659.x: I'm getting a comprehensive health checkup next week.

T3-1660.m: to synthesize, to put together, to sum up
T3-1660.x: We'll make a decision after putting together everyone's opinions.
T3-1660.t: Pronounced [종하파다]: ㅂ + ㅎ merge into ㅍ.

T3-1661.m: to lead, to take the initiative, to spearhead
T3-1661.e: Literally 'to guide as the main one'.

T3-1662.x: Our company values teamwork above all else.
T3-1662.t: A formal, written word; in conversation people often say 중요하게 생각하다.

T3-1663.e: Literally 'power to create ideas'. -력 = ability: 영향력, 능력.

T3-1664.ex: 그 학생은 항상 창의적인 아이디어를 내요.
T3-1664.x: That student always comes up with creative ideas.

T3-1665.m: to take responsibility for, to be responsible for
T3-1665.x: I'll take responsibility for my own mistake.
T3-1665.e: 책임 'responsibility' + native 지다 'to bear on one's back'.
T3-1665.t: Pronounced [채김지다]: the ㄱ batchim moves to the next syllable.

T3-1667.ex: 요즘은 친환경 제품을 사는 사람이 많아요.
T3-1667.x: These days a lot of people buy eco-friendly products.

T3-1668.x: Bicycles are an eco-friendly means of transportation with no exhaust fumes.
T3-1668.e: 친환경 'eco-friendly' + -적; used as an adjective with 인 or 으로.

T3-1669.ex: 특정 음식에 알레르기가 있으면 말해 주세요.
T3-1669.x: Please let us know if you're allergic to any particular food.
T3-1669.t: Almost always used right before a noun (특정 사람, 특정 지역); pronounced [특쩡].

T3-1670.x: We need to let go of prejudices against foreigners.

T3-1671.m: to be evaluated, to be rated, to be recognized
T3-1671.x: That movie was rated as a masterpiece.
T3-1671.e: 평가 'evaluation' + 받다 'to receive' = to receive an evaluation.
T3-1671.t: Pronounced [평까받따]; -받다 makes a passive meaning, like 사랑받다 'be loved'.

T3-1672.x: She has broad experience, so she gives good advice.
T3-1672.e: 폭 'width' + native 넓다 'wide' — literally 'wide in width'.
T3-1672.t: Pronounced [퐁널따]: ㄱ becomes ㅇ before ㄴ, and ㄼ sounds as ㄹ.

T3-1673.x: I felt I'd hit my physical limit, so I took a short break.

T3-1674.ex: 이 가게는 품질도 좋고 가격도 합리적이에요.
T3-1674.x: This store has good quality and reasonable prices too.
T3-1674.t: Pronounced [함니적] — nasalization; 합리적인 가격 is a very common phrase for 'reasonable price'.

T3-1675.x: This sentence is a bit hard to interpret.

T3-1676.x: In this game, teamwork with your friends is important.
T3-1676.t: Pronounced [협똥]: ㄷ after ㅂ becomes tense.

T3-1677.ex: 어린 시절은 성격 형성에 큰 영향을 줘요.
T3-1677.x: Childhood has a big influence on the formation of personality.

T3-1678.x: Please write the report in the set format.
T3-1678.t: 형식적 often means 'just for show': 형식적인 인사 'a perfunctory greeting'.

T3-1679.x: My family was struggling financially, so I worked part-time.
T3-1679.e: 형 'shape' + 편 'convenience': the shape your life is in right now.
T3-1679.t: 형편이 어렵다 is a polite, indirect way to say a family is poor.

T3-1680.x: I became convinced that he was the culprit.
T3-1680.t: Pronounced [확씬]; common phrases: 확신이 들다 'become convinced', 확신이 없다 'not sure'.

T3-1681.m: to be convinced, to be sure, to be certain
T3-1681.ex: 저는 우리 팀이 이길 거라고 확신해요.
T3-1681.x: I'm sure our team will win.

T3-9001.x: Could I get a straw for the iced americano?
T3-9001.e: Native word: 빨다 'to suck' + 대 'stick, tube'.
T3-9001.t: Pronounced [빨때]. Many Korean cafés now hand out paper straws (종이 빨대) instead of plastic ones.

T3-9002.ex: 캐리어에 짐을 다 넣었는데 안 닫혀요.
T3-9002.x: I put all my stuff in the suitcase, but it won't close.
T3-9002.e: Konglish from English 'carrier'; English speakers say 'suitcase' or 'rolling luggage'.
T3-9002.t: A cabin-size suitcase is 기내용 캐리어.

T3-9003.t: As a verb: 체크인하다. Also used for flights at the airport.

T3-9004.ex: 내일 아침 열한 시까지 체크아웃해야 해요.
T3-9004.x: We have to check out by 11 tomorrow morning.
T3-9004.t: Late check-out is 레이트 체크아웃. Many hotels will keep your bags after check-out: 짐 좀 맡겨도 될까요?

T3-9005.x: I lost my key card, so I called the front desk.
T3-9005.t: The standard spelling is 프런트, but 프론트 is very common on signs.

T3-9006.ex: 우리는 십 년 넘게 우정을 지켜 왔어요.
T3-9006.x: We've kept our friendship going for more than ten years.
T3-9006.t: Close friends often get 우정 반지 (friendship rings) or go on a 우정 여행 (friendship trip).

T3-9007.m: budae-jjigae (army stew with ham and sausage)
T3-9007.x: We add ramyeon noodles to our budae-jjigae.
T3-9007.e: 부대 'military unit' + 찌개 'stew'. It began after the Korean War with ham and sausages from US army bases.
T3-9007.t: Adding 라면 사리 (a block of instant noodles) is almost standard.

T3-9008.x: After work, I had some soju at a street tent bar.
T3-9008.e: Literally 'cloth-covered horse cart': a tented stall selling snacks and drinks.
T3-9008.t: Often shortened to 포차. Many indoor bars also use 포차 in their names.

T3-9009.x: In winter, I crave the hotteok sold on the street.
T3-9009.e: 호 'foreign (Chinese)' + 떡 'rice cake' — introduced by Chinese merchants.
T3-9009.t: Filled with brown sugar, cinnamon and nuts. Bite carefully: the melted syrup is very hot.

T3-9010.ex: 겨울이 되면 동네에 붕어빵 가게가 생겨요.
T3-9010.x: When winter comes, bungeoppang stands pop up in the neighborhood.
T3-9010.e: 붕어 'crucian carp' + 빵 'bread' — named for its shape; there's no fish inside.
T3-9010.t: Usually filled with sweet red bean (팥) or custard (슈크림). People jokingly debate whether to eat the head or tail first.

T3-9011.m: food eaten with alcohol, bar snacks
T3-9011.x: What would be good to eat with beer?
T3-9011.e: Literally 'press down the alcohol' — food that softens the drink.
T3-9011.t: Korean bars expect you to order 안주; drinking without food is unusual.

T3-9012.m: to get drunk, be drunk; to be intoxicated (by)
T3-9012.ex: 어제 술에 너무 취해서 기억이 안 나요.
T3-9012.x: I got so drunk yesterday that I can't remember anything.
T3-9012.t: Use the past form for being drunk now: 취했어요 'I'm drunk'. Also figurative: 분위기에 취하다 'be carried away by the mood'.

T3-9013.x: The weather's nice, so how about chicken and beer by the Han River?
T3-9013.t: A favorite while watching sports or picnicking by the Han River; chicken can be delivered right to the park.

T3-9014.ex: 짜장면 두 개하고 탕수육 하나 주세요.
T3-9014.x: Two jajangmyeon and one sweet and sour pork, please.
T3-9014.t: The famous debate: 부먹 (pour the sauce on) or 찍먹 (dip into the sauce)?

T3-9015.x: We ordered jokbal as a late-night snack.
T3-9015.e: 족 'foot' + 발 'foot' — the Sino-Korean and native words together.
T3-9015.t: Pronounced [족빨]. Usually wrapped in lettuce and dipped in salted shrimp sauce (새우젓).

T3-9016.x: I ordered tteokbokki through a delivery app.
T3-9016.t: Apps show reviews and the delivery fee (배달비); many restaurants have a minimum order (최소 주문 금액).

T3-9017.x: Kkakdugi goes really well with seolleongtang.
T3-9017.e: Native word linked to 깍둑 'in chunky cubes', as in 깍둑썰기 'dicing'.
T3-9017.t: Pronounced [깍뚜기]. Casually, it also means a kid who can join either team in a game.

T3-9018.x: I added a little more chili powder to the kimchi stew.
T3-9018.e: 고추 'chili pepper' + 가루 'powder', joined with ㅅ.
T3-9018.t: Pronounced [고추까루] or [고춛까루]. It's the key ingredient that makes kimchi red.

T3-9019.m: namul (seasoned vegetable side dish); edible greens
T3-9019.ex: 엄마가 만든 나물 반찬이 제일 맛있어요.
T3-9019.x: The namul side dishes my mom makes are the best.
T3-9019.e: Native word for edible greens and wild herbs, and the dishes made from them.
T3-9019.t: Usually blanched and seasoned with sesame oil and garlic. 콩나물 (bean sprouts) is the most common kind.

T3-9020.ex: 더운 날에는 친구랑 빙수를 나눠 먹어요.
T3-9020.x: On hot days, I share bingsu with a friend.
T3-9020.t: The classic is 팥빙수 with sweet red beans. One bowl is usually shared by two or more people.

T3-9021.ex: 이 가게 마카롱은 크림이 정말 많아요.
T3-9021.x: The macarons at this shop have tons of cream.
T3-9021.t: Korea's thick, overfilled version is jokingly called 뚱카롱 (뚱뚱하다 'fat' + 마카롱).

T3-9022.x: I ordered an ice cream waffle at the café.
T3-9022.t: Street-stall 와플 in Korea is often folded around whipped cream and jam.

T3-9023.x: The day before Chuseok, I made songpyeon with my family.
T3-9023.e: 송 'pine' + 편 'rice cake' — steamed on a bed of pine needles.
T3-9023.t: You shape songpyeon by hand: 송편을 빚다. An old saying goes that if you make pretty songpyeon, you'll have a pretty daughter.

T3-9024.ex: 추석 밤에 보름달을 보면서 소원을 빌었어요.
T3-9024.x: On Chuseok night, I made a wish while looking at the full moon.
T3-9024.e: 보름 'the 15th day of the lunar month' + 달 'moon'.
T3-9024.t: Pronounced [보름딸]. Making a wish on the full moon is a Chuseok and 정월 대보름 tradition.

T3-9025.ex: 한복을 입으면 경복궁에 무료로 들어갈 수 있어요.
T3-9025.x: If you wear hanbok, you can get into Gyeongbokgung for free.
T3-9025.t: Pronounced [경복꿍]. Built in 1395 as the main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty.

T3-9026.x: After working out, I sweated it out in the sauna.
T3-9026.t: In Korea 사우나 often means the whole bathhouse, not just the hot room, and many bathhouses have 사우나 in their name.

T3-9027.x: At a jjimjilbang, sikhye with baked eggs is the best.
T3-9027.t: Pronounced [시켸] or [시케]. Made by steeping cooked rice in malt water, served cold with grains of rice floating in it.

T3-9028.x: I went to see the fireworks on the Han River.
T3-9028.t: Pronounced [불꼰노리]. Seoul's big fireworks festival on the Han River each autumn draws huge crowds.

T3-9029.m: food, things to eat (at a festival or market)
T3-9029.ex: 이 축제에는 맛있는 먹거리가 정말 많아요.
T3-9029.x: There are lots of tasty things to eat at this festival.
T3-9029.e: 먹다 'to eat' + -거리 'material, stuff for', as in 볼거리 'things to see'.
T3-9029.t: Pronounced [먹꺼리]. Long considered nonstandard, it was accepted as standard in 2011 alongside 먹을거리.

T3-9030.ex: 결혼식 때 입을 웨딩드레스를 고르러 갔어요.
T3-9030.x: I went to choose a wedding dress to wear at the wedding.
T3-9030.t: Brides usually rent rather than buy, and many couples wear it months earlier for studio wedding photos (웨딩 촬영).

T3-9031.ex: 여름 휴가 때 부산 해운대에 놀러 갔어요.
T3-9031.x: During summer vacation I went to Haeundae in Busan.
T3-9031.t: Korea's best-known beach. 해운대 해수욕장 = Haeundae Beach.

T3-9032.ex: 제주도에 가면 한라산에 꼭 올라가 보고 싶어요.
T3-9032.x: When I go to Jeju, I really want to climb Hallasan.
T3-9032.e: Traditionally read as 'mountain high enough to pull down the Milky Way'.
T3-9032.t: Pronounced [할라산]. At 1,947 m it is the highest mountain in South Korea.

T3-9033.x: My grandmother still speaks her hometown dialect.
T3-9033.e: Native word for regional speech; the formal term is 방언.
T3-9033.t: Say 사투리를 쓰다 'to speak in dialect'. Standard Korean (표준어) is based on Seoul speech.

T3-9034.m: to debut, to make one's debut
T3-9034.x: That group debuted three years ago.
T3-9034.t: K-pop idols usually train for years as trainees (연습생) before they debut. 데뷔 무대 = debut stage.

T3-9035.x: My favorite group is making a comeback next month.
T3-9035.e: From English 'comeback'. Konglish: in K-pop it means any new release, not only a return after a long break.
T3-9035.t: Used as 컴백하다. 컴백 무대 = the first TV performances of a new release.

T3-9036.x: As soon as the new song came out, it hit number one on the music charts.
T3-9036.t: 곡 is the formal word and counter for songs: 이번 앨범에는 열 곡이 있어요.

T3-9037.ex: 고등학교 때 그 가수의 팬클럽에 가입했어요.
T3-9037.x: In high school I joined that singer's fan club.
T3-9037.t: Official fan clubs usually charge a membership fee, which can give priority in concert ticketing.

T3-9038.ex: 콘서트 표가 오 분 만에 매진됐어요.
T3-9038.x: The concert tickets sold out in five minutes.
T3-9038.t: Used as 매진되다: 표가 매진됐어요 'the tickets sold out'. 매진 임박 = almost sold out.

T3-9039.ex: 관객들이 앙코르를 외치자 가수가 다시 나왔어요.
T3-9039.x: When the audience shouted for an encore, the singer came back out.
T3-9039.t: 앙코르 공연 can also mean extra shows added because of demand.

T3-9040.ex: 다음 달에 첫 팬 미팅이 열린대요.
T3-9040.x: I heard their first fan meeting is being held next month.
T3-9040.e: From English 'fan' + 'meeting'. Konglish: an event where stars talk, play games and perform for fans.
T3-9040.t: Often written without a space: 팬미팅.

T3-9041.ex: 이번 주 음악 차트 순위가 많이 바뀌었어요.
T3-9041.x: The music chart rankings changed a lot this week.
T3-9041.t: Ranks use -위: 1위, 2위. 순위가 오르다 / 떨어지다 = to rise / fall in the rankings.

T3-9042.x: The newly released song went to No. 1 on the chart.
T3-9042.t: Also used for a patient's medical chart at a hospital.

T3-9043.ex: 이 동작은 어려워서 몇 번 더 연습해야 해요.
T3-9043.x: This move is hard, so I need to practice it a few more times.
T3-9043.t: In dance class you'll hear 동작을 크게 하세요 'make your moves bigger'. 동작이 빠르다 / 느리다 = to be quick / slow in moving.

T3-9044.ex: 가수가 되고 싶어서 기획사 오디션을 봤어요.
T3-9044.x: I wanted to become a singer, so I auditioned for an agency.
T3-9044.t: The verb is 보다: 오디션을 보다 'to audition'. To pass is 오디션에 붙다 or 합격하다.

T3-9045.ex: 한국 드라마를 자막 없이 보고 싶어요.
T3-9045.x: I want to watch Korean dramas without subtitles.
T3-9045.t: Korean variety shows are famous for colorful on-screen captions, which are also called 자막.

T3-9046.x: We promised to meet on the day of the first snow.
T3-9046.t: Pronounced [천눈]. Romantic in Korean culture: couples promise to meet when the first snow falls, and folk belief says your love comes true if your balsam nail dye (봉숭아 물) lasts until then.

T3-9047.x: I think our meeting was fate.
T3-9047.t: 운명적인 만남 'a fated meeting' is a classic K-drama phrase. 인연 stresses the bond between people; 운명 is fate in general.

T3-9048.ex: 저는 슬픈 영화보다 로맨스 영화를 좋아해요.
T3-9048.x: I like romance movies more than sad movies.
T3-9048.t: Combines with other genres, as in 로맨스 판타지; 로맨틱 코미디 is shortened to 로코.

T3-9049.ex: 판타지 드라마라서 주인공이 시간 여행을 해요.
T3-9049.x: It's a fantasy drama, so the main character travels through time.
T3-9049.t: Popular mixes include 로맨스 판타지 'romance fantasy', often adapted from web novels and webtoons.

T3-9050.ex: 이 영화는 액션 장면이 정말 멋있어요.
T3-9050.x: The action scenes in this movie are really cool.
T3-9050.t: On film sets, the director calls 레디, 액션! 'Ready, action!'

T3-9051.ex: 그 드라마 마지막 대사가 아직도 기억나요.
T3-9051.x: I still remember the last line of that drama.
T3-9051.t: 대사를 외우다 = to memorize one's lines. Homonym: 대사 (大使) also means 'ambassador'.

T3-9052.m: season (of a series); season (time of year)
T3-9052.x: Season 2 of that drama is coming out soon.
T3-9052.t: Also used for times of year: 휴가 시즌 'vacation season', 시즌 한정 'seasonal limited edition'.

T3-9053.ex: 주말이면 공원에서 거리 공연이 자주 열려요.
T3-9053.x: On weekends there are often street performances in the park.
T3-9053.t: Common in news and on signs; in casual talk people often say 버스킹. A performance is held is 공연이 열리다.

T3-9054.m: Hongdae (Seoul area known for indie music and busking)
T3-9054.x: I hung out with my friends in Hongdae on Friday night.
T3-9054.e: Short for 홍익대학교 (Hongik University): 홍익 'broadly benefit (people)' + 대(학교) 'university'.
T3-9054.t: Means both the university and the lively area around it, full of clubs, cafés and buskers; the main stop is 홍대입구역.

T3-9055.x: I played games all night at a PC bang with my friend.
T3-9055.t: Often written PC방. Most charge by the hour and deliver snacks like ramyeon to your seat.

T3-9056.m: character (in a game or story); mascot character
T3-9056.ex: 이 게임에서는 캐릭터를 직접 꾸밀 수 있어요.
T3-9056.x: In this game you can customize your character yourself.
T3-9056.t: Also used for cute mascot figures: 캐릭터 상품 = character goods. For someone's personality, use 성격.

T3-9057.ex: 주말 내내 게임해서 레벨을 많이 올렸어요.
T3-9057.x: I played games all weekend and leveled up a lot.
T3-9057.t: 레벨을 올리다 or 레벨 업 하다 = to level up; also for skill: 레벨 테스트 = placement test.

T3-9058.m: item (in a game); must-have product; business idea
T3-9058.ex: 이 아이템을 쓰면 캐릭터가 더 강해져요.
T3-9058.x: If you use this item, your character gets stronger.
T3-9058.t: Beyond games, 필수 아이템 means a 'must-have' and 창업 아이템 a business idea.

T3-9059.ex: 제가 올린 사진에 좋아요 좀 눌러 주세요.
T3-9059.x: Please like the photo I posted.
T3-9059.e: The polite form of 좋다 'to be good', used as a noun for the 'like' button.
T3-9059.t: Pronounced [조아요]. Like a post is 좋아요를 누르다; 좋아요 수 = number of likes.

T3-9060.ex: 그 친구는 SNS 팔로워가 만 명이 넘어요.
T3-9060.x: That friend has over ten thousand followers on social media.
T3-9060.t: 팔로우하다 = to follow; 맞팔 (casual) = following each other.

T3-9061.m: review (written by a customer or attendee)
T3-9061.x: The reviews were good, so I bought this bag.
T3-9061.t: Very common online: 구매 후기 'purchase review', 여행 후기 'travel write-up'. 리뷰 is used the same way.

T3-9062.forms: casual exclamation · 대박이다 · 대박(이) 나다 (to be a big hit)
T3-9062.x: Awesome! I managed to book concert tickets.
T3-9062.e: Often explained as 대 'big' + 박 'gourd', recalling the treasure-filled gourds in the folktale of Heungbu; the true origin is uncertain.
T3-9062.t: Casual; works for good or shocking news. 대박 나세요! = 'Wishing you huge success!' (e.g. to a new business).

T3-9063.ex: 답장할 때 귀여운 이모티콘을 자주 써요.
T3-9063.x: I often use cute emoticons when I reply.
T3-9063.t: In Korea it covers emoji and the animated character stickers bought for messenger apps.

T3-9064.ex: 단톡방 알림이 계속 와서 꺼 놨어요.
T3-9064.x: Group chat notifications kept coming, so I turned them off.
T3-9064.e: Native noun from 알리다 'to let know'.
T3-9064.t: Turn on/off notifications is 알림을 켜다/끄다. Don't confuse with 알람 'alarm (clock)'.

T3-9065.ex: 저희 아파트는 반려동물을 키울 수 있어요.
T3-9065.x: Pets are allowed in our apartment building.
T3-9065.t: Pronounced [발려동물]. Now preferred over 애완동물; also 반려견 'companion dog' and 반려묘 'companion cat'.

T3-9066.x: I always do my skincare before bed.
T3-9066.t: Watch out: 스킨 alone usually means toner in Korea, as in the basic routine 스킨 → 로션.

T3-9067.x: Be sure to put on sunscreen before you go out.
T3-9067.e: Konglish from English 'sun' + 'cream'; English speakers say 'sunscreen'.
T3-9067.t: Put it on is 선크림을 바르다; the formal term is 자외선 차단제 'UV blocker'.

T3-9068.ex: 피곤한 날에는 마스크 팩을 붙이고 쉬어요.
T3-9068.x: On tiring days, I put on a sheet mask and relax.
T3-9068.e: Konglish from English 'mask' + 'pack'; English speakers say 'sheet mask'.
T3-9068.t: Often just 팩; put one on is 팩을 하다/붙이다. Don't confuse with 마스크 alone, which usually means a face covering.

T3-9069.ex: 이 떡집은 우리 엄마 단골 가게예요.
T3-9069.x: This rice cake shop is my mom's regular place.
T3-9069.e: Native word. It first meant the shaman a family always called on (단골무당), then a regular customer or shop.
T3-9069.t: 단골 can mean the person (단골손님) or the place (단골집). Regulars often get a little extra for free, called 서비스 or 덤.

T3-9070.x: My bangs were poking my eyes, so I trimmed them a little.
T3-9070.t: Pronounced [암머리]: ㅍ turns into ㅁ before ㅁ. To get bangs is 앞머리를 내다; to grow them out is 앞머리를 기르다.

T3-9071.ex: 이 코트는 세탁소에 드라이클리닝을 맡겨야 해요.
T3-9071.x: I need to take this coat to the cleaner's for dry cleaning.
T3-9071.t: At the 세탁소, just say 드라이클리닝 해 주세요. Ordinary washing in water is 물세탁.

T3-9072.ex: 에어컨이 고장 나서 수리 기사를 불렀어요.
T3-9072.x: The air conditioner broke down, so I called a repair technician.
T3-9072.e: 수리 'repair' (literally 'mend and put in order') + 기사 'technician'.
T3-9072.t: Address a technician politely as 기사님. Big electronics brands send their own 수리 기사 for home visits after you book through the service center.

T3-9073.ex: 단 걸 많이 먹어서 충치가 생겼어요.
T3-9073.x: I ate a lot of sweets and got a cavity.
T3-9073.e: Literally 'worm tooth', from the old belief that worms ate holes in teeth.
T3-9073.t: A cavity 'forms': 충치가 생기다. Getting one treated is 충치 치료.

T3-9074.ex: 오늘은 안경 대신 렌즈를 끼고 왔어요.
T3-9074.x: Today I came wearing contacts instead of glasses.
T3-9074.t: In daily talk 렌즈 usually means contact lenses (콘택트렌즈). Put them in with 끼다, take them out with 빼다.

T3-9075.ex: 다음 주에 과 친구들이랑 엠티 가요.
T3-9075.x: Next week I'm going on an MT with friends from my department.
T3-9075.e: Konglish: from the initials of English 'membership training', also written MT.
T3-9075.t: Usually an overnight trip to a rented country guesthouse with games, cooking and drinking, especially common for freshmen in the spring semester.

T3-9076.ex: 저는 서울에 있는 어학당에서 한국어를 배워요.
T3-9076.x: I'm learning Korean at a university language institute in Seoul.
T3-9076.e: 어학 'language study' + 당 'hall': literally 'language study hall'.
T3-9076.t: Pronounced [어학땅]: ㄷ becomes tense after ㄱ. Most major universities run one, with terms of about ten weeks.

T3-9077.x: We did a dictation in Korean class today.
T3-9077.e: 받다 'receive' + 쓰다 'write' + -기 (noun ending): writing down what you take in by ear.
T3-9077.t: A staple of Korean elementary schools and language classes, since it tests spelling rules where sound and spelling differ.

T3-9078.ex: 시험 전에 문제집을 한 권 다 풀었어요.
T3-9078.x: Before the exam, I worked through a whole workbook.
T3-9078.t: You 'solve' a workbook: 문제집을 풀다. Korean bookstores have whole sections of them for the 수능 and TOPIK.

T3-9079.x: Please check the attached file and get back to me.
T3-9079.e: 첨부 'attaching' (literally 'add and attach') + 파일 from English 'file'.
T3-9079.t: Useful lines: 파일을 첨부했습니다 'I've attached the file'; 첨부 파일이 안 열려요 'The attachment won't open'.

T3-9080.x: I'll send you the meeting materials by messenger.
T3-9080.t: At work 메신저 often means the company's internal chat tool, used for quick questions instead of email.

T3-9081.ex: 다음 달에 퇴사하고 잠시 쉬려고 해요.
T3-9081.x: I'm going to leave the company next month and take a short break.
T3-9081.e: Literally 'leaving the company'. Opposite: 입사 'joining a company'.
T3-9081.t: 퇴사 is quitting for good, while 퇴근 is just leaving work for the day. Verb: 퇴사하다.

T3-9082.x: How much is the hourly wage for this convenience store job?
T3-9082.t: Korea's legal minimum wage (최저 임금) is set each year as an hourly rate. Homonym: 시급 'urgent' uses different hanja.

T3-9083.x: I made a wish and blew out the candles on the cake.
T3-9083.t: Pronounced [초뿔]: the ㅅ added between the two parts makes the ㅂ tense. Blowing out candles is 촛불을 끄다, literally 'turn off the candles'.

T3-9084.ex: 생일 아침에 엄마가 미역국을 끓여 주셨어요.
T3-9084.x: On my birthday morning, my mom made me seaweed soup.
T3-9084.t: Pronounced [미역꾹]: ㄱ becomes tense after ㄱ. Mothers eat it after giving birth, which is why it is eaten on birthdays. 미역국을 먹다 is also slang for failing an exam; it is usually explained by slippery seaweed suggesting 미끄러지다 'to slip', but that is a popular explanation, not a proven origin.

T3-9085.x: My grandmother passed away, so I went to the funeral hall today.
T3-9085.t: Pronounced [장녜식짱]: ㄹ becomes ㄴ after ㅇ, and ㅈ turns tense after ㄱ. Most Korean funerals are held in funeral halls attached to hospitals, usually over three days.

T3-9086.x: It's time to change the baby's diaper.
T3-9086.t: 'Change a diaper' is 기저귀를 갈다 (갈다 'to replace'). Disposable ones are 일회용 기저귀; cloth ones are 천 기저귀.

T3-9087.x: Every morning I drop my child off at daycare and go to work.
T3-9087.t: Pronounced [어리니집]: the ㄴ links into the next syllable. Daycare takes children from infancy up to age five, while 유치원 is for ages three to five.

T3-9088.x: On graduation day I gave my friend a bouquet.
T3-9088.t: Pronounced [꼳따발]: final ㅊ sounds like ㄷ and makes the next ㄷ tense. Bouquets are a must at Korean graduations, and flower stalls pop up outside schools on the day.

T3-9089.x: I received my diploma from the principal at the graduation ceremony.
T3-9089.t: Pronounced [조럽짱]: ㄹ links into 업, and ㅈ turns tense after ㅂ. For job or visa paperwork you usually submit a 졸업증명서 (official certificate of graduation).

T3-9090.x: After the graduation ceremony, I took a commemorative photo with my family.
T3-9090.t: Used for any photo marking an occasion or a visit. To ask a passer-by: 사진 좀 찍어 주시겠어요?

T3-9091.x: The accident was caught on the dashcam just as it happened.
T3-9091.e: From English 'black box'. Konglish: in Korea it usually means a car dashcam, not a flight recorder.
T3-9091.t: Almost every car in Korea has one, and its footage is often the key evidence in deciding who caused an accident.

T3-9092.x: If there's a fire, evacuate quickly by the stairs.
T3-9092.t: A key word in disaster alert texts. The destination takes (으)로: 안전한 곳으로 대피하다 'evacuate to a safe place'.

T3-9093.ex: 주말에 산에 가면 화려한 등산복을 입은 사람이 많아요.
T3-9093.x: When you go to the mountains on the weekend, lots of people are wearing colorful hiking gear.
T3-9093.t: Bright, high-tech outdoor wear is famously popular in Korea, and many middle-aged people wear it even off the trail.

T3-9094.x: I climbed the mountain in my new hiking boots.
T3-9094.t: Shoes take 신다 'to put on (footwear)', not 입다: 등산화를 신다.

T3-9095.x: It's really hard to book a campground on weekends.
T3-9095.t: Popular campgrounds open online reservations at a set time and can be fully booked within minutes for summer weekends.

T3-9096.x: In the evening we had a barbecue at the campground.
T3-9096.t: The standard spelling is 바비큐, but you'll often see 바베큐 on signs and menus.

T3-9097.ex: 여름이 되면 해수욕장에 사람이 정말 많아요.
T3-9097.x: In summer the beaches get really crowded.
T3-9097.t: Pronounced [해수욕짱]: ㅈ becomes tense after ㄱ. Most officially open only in summer, roughly July to August, when lifeguards are on duty.

T3-9098.x: The child played in the sea on a swim ring.
T3-9098.e: From English 'tube'. Konglish: in Korea it usually means an inflatable swim ring.
T3-9098.t: Floating on one is 튜브를 타다, literally 'to ride a tube'.

T3-9099.x: The kids are playing in the water at the valley stream.
T3-9099.t: Pronounced [물로리]: ㄴ becomes ㄹ after ㄹ. Splashing in a mountain stream is a classic Korean summer family outing.

T3-9100.ex: 친구가 노래할 때 제가 탬버린을 쳤어요.
T3-9100.x: I played the tambourine while my friend sang.
T3-9100.t: Most 노래방 rooms have a couple; shaking one to cheer on whoever is singing is part of the fun.

T3-9101.x: There was a come-from-behind home run in the last inning.
T3-9101.t: Pronounced [홈넌]: ㄹ becomes ㄴ after ㅁ. 'Hit a home run' is 홈런을 치다.

T3-9102.x: We spread a mat on the grass in the park and sat down.
T3-9102.e: Native word; originally a mat woven from rush stems. 자리 means 'mat, seat'.
T3-9102.t: Pronounced [돋짜리]: ㅅ sounds like ㄷ and makes the next ㅈ tense. Spreading one is 돗자리를 깔다; Han River parks fill with them on warm evenings.

T3-9103.x: We sat on the grass and ate our packed lunch.
T3-9103.e: Native word. 잔디밭 = a lawn, a grassy field (밭 'field').
T3-9103.t: 풀 is grass or weeds in general; 잔디 is the short, planted kind. Keep-off signs say 잔디에 들어가지 마세요.

T3-9104.x: I went on five rides at the amusement park.
T3-9104.t: Pronounced [노리기구]: the ㄹ links into the next syllable. Rides are 'ridden': 놀이기구를 타다.

T3-9105.x: The roller coaster was so scary that I screamed.
T3-9105.t: Older people may call it 청룡열차 'blue dragon train', after one of Korea's first coasters.

T3-9106.x: I saw lots of amazing fish at the aquarium.
T3-9106.e: Literally 'water-family hall': 수족 means creatures that live in water.
T3-9106.t: Pronounced [수족꽌]: ㄱ makes the next ㄱ tense. Big ones often call themselves 아쿠아리움.

T3-9107.ex: 사진 찍을 때 귀여운 포즈를 취해 보세요.
T3-9107.x: Try striking a cute pose when you take a picture.
T3-9107.t: 'Strike a pose' is 포즈를 취하다. Classic Korean photo poses are the V-sign and the finger heart (손가락 하트).

T3-9108.ex: 이 필터를 쓰면 피부가 더 좋아 보여요.
T3-9108.x: If you use this filter, your skin looks better.
T3-9108.t: Korean camera apps are known for beauty filters. #노필터 'no filter' tags an unedited photo.

T3-9109.x: I went to a photo studio to get my passport photo taken.
T3-9109.t: The place to get ID and passport photos (증명사진); most studios retouch them for you.

T3-9110.e: From 달다 'sweet' with -콤-, which adds a pleasant, appealing tone.
T3-9110.t: Also used figuratively: 달콤한 목소리 'a sweet voice', 달콤한 말 'sweet talk'.

T3-9111.x: Please flip the meat with the tongs.
T3-9111.e: 집다 'to pick up' + -게, an ending for tools.
T3-9111.t: Pronounced [집께]: ㄱ becomes tense after ㅂ. At Korean BBQ restaurants each table gets tongs and scissors (가위) for cooking and cutting the meat.

T3-9112.ex: 상추에 고기를 올려서 쌈을 싸 먹어요.
T3-9112.x: I put meat on lettuce, wrap it up and eat it.
T3-9112.t: 'Make a wrap' is 쌈을 싸다. Make it bite-sized and eat it in one mouthful.

T3-9113.x: Meat tastes great dipped in ssamjang.
T3-9113.t: It's 된장 mixed with 고추장, garlic and sesame oil. Also great as a dip for raw garlic, chili peppers or cucumber sticks.

T3-9114.ex: 저는 해산물을 좋아해서 새우랑 오징어를 자주 먹어요.
T3-9114.x: I like seafood, so I often eat shrimp and squid.
T3-9114.t: In dish names the short form 해물 is used: 해물파전 'seafood pancake', 해물탕 'seafood stew'.

T3-9115.x: I'm a vegetarian, so I don't eat meat.
T3-9115.t: Pronounced [채식쭈의자] or [채식쭈이자]: ㅈ turns tense after ㄱ, and 의 after the first syllable may sound like 이. Many Korean dishes use meat or fish broth, so ask: 고기 들어가요?

T3-9116.x: At the temple, a monk served us tea.
T3-9116.e: Usually traced to 승님: 승 (僧) 'monk' + honorific -님, with the ㅇ dropped to give 스님.
T3-9116.t: Use it as a form of address too: 스님, 안녕하세요. 승려 is the formal or written word.

T3-9117.x: I went to the temple and made a wish to the Buddha.
T3-9117.e: 부처 'Buddha' + honorific -님; 부처 came from 'Buddha' via Chinese.
T3-9117.t: His birthday, the 8th day of the 4th lunar month, is a public holiday called 부처님오신날, when temples hang lotus lanterns.

T3-9118.ex: 이번 휴가에는 절에서 템플스테이를 해 보고 싶어요.
T3-9118.x: This vacation I'd like to try a temple stay at a Buddhist temple.
T3-9118.e: From English 'temple' + 'stay'; the name was created for a Korean program that opened temples to visitors in 2002.
T3-9118.t: Guests usually wear temple clothes, join the dawn chanting, eat a silent temple meal (발우공양) and try meditation; many temples run programs in English.

T3-9119.ex: 자기 전에 십 분씩 명상을 하면 마음이 편해져요.
T3-9119.x: If I meditate for ten minutes before bed, my mind feels at ease.
T3-9119.e: Literally 'deep thinking': 冥 'dark, deep' + 想 'thought'.

T3-9120.m: hanok village (area of traditional Korean houses)
T3-9120.ex: 전주 한옥마을에서 한복을 입고 사진을 찍었어요.
T3-9120.x: I wore hanbok and took photos in the Jeonju hanok village.
T3-9120.t: Pronounced [하농마을]: ㄱ becomes ㅇ before ㅁ. In villages like Seoul's Bukchon people still live in the houses, so visitors are asked to keep their voices down.

T3-9121.x: I learned kicks for the first time at the taekwondo school.
T3-9121.t: Basic taekwondo kicks: 앞차기 'front kick', 옆차기 'side kick', 돌려차기 'roundhouse kick'.

T3-9122.x: I'm a Dragon. What's your zodiac sign?
T3-9122.e: Native word whose basic meaning is 'band, belt' (허리띠 'waist belt'); after an animal name it marks your birth-year sign: 쥐띠, 소띠, 용띠.
T3-9122.t: Asking 무슨 띠예요? is an indirect way to find out someone's age. Two people 12 years apart share the same animal and are called 띠동갑.

T3-9123.forms: set phrase: 옛날 옛적에 … 살았어요 (storytelling style: 살았답니다)
T3-9123.m: once upon a time, long, long ago
T3-9123.ex: 옛날 옛적에 깊은 산속에 호랑이 한 마리가 살았어요.
T3-9123.x: Once upon a time, a tiger lived deep in the mountains.
T3-9123.e: 옛날 'the old days' + 옛적 'olden times' + 에 'at': two near-synonyms stacked for storytelling rhythm.
T3-9123.t: Pronounced [옌날 옏쩌게]: the final ㅅ becomes ㄴ before ㄴ, and ㅈ turns tense after it. Folktales often go on with 호랑이 담배 피우던 시절에 'back when tigers smoked'.

T3-9124.ex: 할머니가 도깨비가 나오는 옛날이야기를 해 주셨어요.
T3-9124.x: My grandmother told me an old story with a dokkaebi in it.
T3-9124.e: Native word of uncertain origin for a creature of Korean folklore.
T3-9124.t: A 도깨비 is a mischievous trickster rather than an evil spirit: in tales it loves ssireum wrestling and carries a magic club (도깨비방망이) that conjures up gold.

T3-9125.ex: 밤에 그 학교에서 귀신을 봤다는 소문이 있어요.
T3-9125.x: There's a rumor that someone saw a ghost at that school at night.
T3-9125.t: The classic Korean ghost is a long-haired woman in white (처녀귀신). 귀신같이 means 'uncannily': 귀신같이 알아요 'knows it uncannily well'.

T3-9126.ex: 요즘 서울 집값이 너무 올라서 걱정이에요.
T3-9126.x: I'm worried because house prices in Seoul have gone up so much lately.
T3-9126.t: Pronounced [집깝]: ㄱ becomes tense after ㅂ. News headlines often say 집값이 폭등하다 'house prices soar'.

T3-9127.ex: 요즘은 인공지능으로 번역도 하고 그림도 그려요.
T3-9127.x: These days people translate and even draw pictures with AI.
T3-9127.t: In everyday speech people also just say AI (에이아이).

T3-9128.x: I watered the potted plant on the balcony.
T3-9128.t: 화분 means both the pot and the plant in it: 화분을 키우다 'grow a potted plant'. A potted plant is a classic housewarming or shop-opening gift.

T3-9129.ex: 맑은 날 밤에는 시골에서 별자리를 볼 수 있어요.
T3-9129.x: On clear nights you can see the constellations in the countryside.
T3-9129.e: Native: 별 'star' + 자리 'place, seat' — a star's place in the sky.
T3-9129.t: Pronounced [별짜리]: the ㅈ of 자리 is said tense in this compound (a sai-sori effect, not a rule triggered by ㄹ). It also means a Western star sign: 무슨 별자리예요? 'What's your star sign?'

T3-9130.x: I read web novels on my phone on the way to and from work.
T3-9130.t: Pronounced [웹쏘설]: ㅅ becomes tense after ㅂ. Web novels come out in short episodes on apps, usually with the first ones free; hits are often adapted into webtoons and dramas.

T3-9131.ex: 친구들이 재미있는 영상을 보며 깔깔 웃었어요.
T3-9131.x: My friends were cackling with laughter while watching a funny video.
T3-9131.e: 의성어 (sound word) for high, loud laughter, often of children or girls. Its dark-vowel partner 껄껄 is a deep, hearty laugh.
T3-9131.t: Verb: 깔깔거리다 or 깔깔대다 'to laugh loudly, cackle'.

T3-9132.x: My little brother played a prank and giggled 'hee-hee'.
T3-9132.e: 의성어 (sound word) for a cheeky, mischievous giggle, typical of children.
T3-9132.t: Adults use it mostly in texts to sound playful or soften a tease.

T3-9133.x: The child fell down and cried loudly.
T3-9133.e: 의성어 (sound word) for loud, open crying. Its bright-vowel partner 앙앙 is a small child's wail.
T3-9133.t: Almost always paired with 울다: 엉엉 울다 'to bawl'. Quiet sniffling is 훌쩍훌쩍.

T3-9134.e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating a rooster's crow.
T3-9134.t: Animal sounds usually take 하고 울다: 꼬끼오 하고 울다 'to crow'. Chicks say 삐약삐약.

T3-9135.x: A cow is mooing in the field.
T3-9135.e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating the low call of a cow or calf.

T3-9136.x: The pigs are oinking as they eat their feed.
T3-9136.e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating a pig's grunt.
T3-9136.t: Verb: 꿀꿀거리다 'to oink'. Casual 꿀꿀하다 means 'to feel gloomy': 날씨가 꿀꿀해요.

T3-9137.x: Every morning sparrows chirp outside the window.
T3-9137.e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating the chirp of a sparrow or other small bird.

T3-9138.ex: 비가 오면 논에서 개구리가 개굴개굴 울어요.
T3-9138.x: When it rains, frogs croak in the rice paddies.
T3-9138.e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating a frog's croak.
T3-9138.t: A typical summer-night sound in the countryside, and the opening of the children's song 개굴개굴 개구리.

T3-9139.x: At the zoo, the tiger let out a roar.
T3-9139.e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating a tiger's roar.
T3-9139.t: Parents shout 어흥! playfully to 'scare' small children, like English 'Rawr!'.

T3-9140.x: Early in the morning, the phone rang.
T3-9140.e: 의성어 (sound word) for the ringing of an old-style telephone or alarm clock.
T3-9140.t: Also the classic bicycle bell, as in the children's song 따르릉 따르릉 비켜나세요.

T3-9141.e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating a two-tone doorbell or chime.
T3-9141.t: 딩동댕 is the chime for a correct answer on quiz shows; a wrong answer gets 땡.

T3-9142.x: The door slammed shut in the wind.
T3-9142.e: 의성어 (sound word) for a loud, sharp bang: a slammed door, a crash or an explosion.
T3-9142.t: Doubled 쾅쾅 means repeated banging: 문을 쾅쾅 두드리다. For a dull, heavy fall, use 쿵.

T3-9143.x: The child fell off the bed with a thud.
T3-9143.e: 의성어 (sound word) for a dull, heavy thud. Its bright-vowel partner 콩 is a small, light bump.
T3-9143.t: Verb: 쿵쿵거리다 'to thump around', a common complaint about noisy upstairs neighbors. 가슴이 쿵 내려앉다 = 'my heart sank'.

T3-9144.x: The kimchi stew is bubbling in the pot.
T3-9144.e: Both 의성어 and 의태어: the sound and look of a small amount of liquid bubbling. Its dark-vowel partner 부글부글 is a bigger, heavier boil, and also describes seething anger.

T3-9145.ex: 길이 막히자 차들이 빵빵 경적을 울렸어요.
T3-9145.x: When traffic jammed, the cars started honking.
T3-9145.e: 의성어 (sound word) imitating a car horn.
T3-9145.t: Verb: 빵빵거리다 'to honk'. Casual 빵빵하다 means 'full, strong': 에어컨이 빵빵해요 'The AC is blasting'.

T3-9146.e: Both 의성어 and 의태어: heavy rain or water streaming down. Its bright-vowel partner 조록조록 is a lighter stream.
T3-9146.t: Pronounced [주룩쭈룩]: the second ㅈ becomes tense after ㄱ. Also used for tears: 눈물이 주룩주룩 흘렀어요.

T3-9147.x: A cold wind is whooshing outside.
T3-9147.e: Both 의성어 and 의태어: the whoosh of a strong wind or of something racing past, as in 차들이 쌩쌩 달려요.
T3-9147.t: Casual 쌩쌩하다 means 'fresh, full of energy': 푹 자서 쌩쌩해요.

T3-9148.m: heavily (snow falling); (cry) one's eyes out; (spend) freely; bang bang
T3-9148.e: Both a sound word (의성어) for bangs, like fireworks, and a manner word (의태어) for something pouring out in great amounts.
T3-9148.t: Also 펑펑 울다 'to cry one's eyes out' and 돈을 펑펑 쓰다 'to spend money like water'.

T3-9149.x: The stream in the valley trickles along.
T3-9149.e: Sound and manner word (의성어·의태어) for a thin stream of water. Bright-vowel 졸졸 is small and gentle; dark-vowel 줄줄 is a heavier flow, as in 땀이 줄줄 흘러요 'sweat is pouring down'.
T3-9149.t: 졸졸 따라다니다 means 'to tag along after someone', like a child following a parent.

T3-9150.x: The sun is really blazing down today.
T3-9150.e: Manner word (의태어) for strong, glaring sunlight with no clouds.
T3-9150.t: Also used as an adjective: 햇볕이 쨍쨍해요 'The sun is blazing.'

T3-9151.x: I tiptoed so the baby wouldn't wake up.
T3-9151.e: Manner word (의태어) for moving quietly so no one notices. Dark-vowel 슬금슬금 is the standard pair, with a more furtive, sly feel.
T3-9151.t: Typically with movement verbs: 살금살금 다가가다 'to creep up on'.

T3-9152.x: The children hold hands and spin round and round.
T3-9152.e: Manner word (의태어) for something turning smoothly again and again. Bright-vowel 뱅글뱅글 describes smaller things spinning.
T3-9152.t: 머리가 빙글빙글 돌아요 'My head is spinning' describes dizziness; 빙글빙글 웃다 is a soft, ongoing smile.

T3-9153.e: Manner word (의태어) for short, light hops with both feet. Dark-vowel 껑충껑충 is for big, long leaps.
T3-9153.t: The standard spelling is 깡충깡충, not the common misspelling 깡총깡총.

T3-9154.x: I swallowed the pill with water in one gulp.
T3-9154.e: Sound and manner word (의성어·의태어) for swallowing at once. Bright-vowel 꼴깍 is a smaller, lighter swallow.
T3-9154.t: 침을 꿀꺽 삼키다 = 'to gulp nervously' or at tempting food. 꿀꺽하다 is also slang for pocketing money dishonestly.

T3-9155.x: I slurped up the hot ramyeon.
T3-9155.e: Sound word (의성어) for sucking in noodles or liquid noisily and quickly.
T3-9155.t: Slurping noodles is generally fine at a Korean table; 후루룩 is part of the fun.

T3-9156.x: The cucumber is fresh, so it's nice and crunchy.
T3-9156.e: Sound word (의성어) for biting into something fresh and juicy, like cucumber, apple or kimchi.
T3-9156.t: Pronounced [아사가삭]: the ㄱ links to the next vowel. 아삭하다 is common: 아삭한 김치 'crisp kimchi'.

T3-9157.x: This rice cake is really chewy.
T3-9157.e: Manner word (의태어) for a springy, elastic texture; a big compliment for 떡, noodles or squid in Korean food.
T3-9157.t: Pronounced [쫄긷쫄긷]: final ㅅ sounds like ㄷ. The short adjective 쫄깃하다 is also very common.

T3-9158.x: The tempura came out nice and crispy.
T3-9158.e: Sound word (의성어) for biting dry, crisp food. Dark-vowel 버석버석 is the coarser, drier sound, like stepping on dry leaves.
T3-9158.t: Pronounced [바삭빠삭]: the final ㄱ makes the next ㅂ tense. 바삭하다 is everyday: 바삭한 치킨 'crispy chicken'.

T3-9159.x: I'm so hungry my stomach is growling.
T3-9159.e: Sound word (의성어) for a rumbling stomach, or liquid gurgling through a narrow opening.
T3-9159.t: Almost always 배에서 꼬르륵 소리가 나다; 배가 꼬르륵거리다 also works.

T3-9160.x: It's my first date, so my heart is pounding.
T3-9160.e: Manner word (의태어) for a heart beating fast and hard from excitement, nerves or fear.
T3-9160.t: The verb 두근거리다 is very common: 가슴이 두근거려요 'My heart is racing.'

T3-9161.x: It was so cold my whole body was shaking.
T3-9161.e: Manner word (의태어) for shaking hard. Bright-vowel 달달 is a smaller tremble: 다리를 달달 떨다.
T3-9161.t: 덜덜거리다 is also used for an old machine or car rattling.

T3-9162.m: to twinkle, to sparkle, to glitter
T3-9162.x: The stars are twinkling in the night sky.
T3-9162.e: Mimetic 반짝 'a brief glint' + -이다, a suffix that turns mimetic words into verbs. Dark-vowel 번쩍이다 is a bigger, stronger flash.
T3-9162.t: Pronounced [반짜기다]: the final ㄱ links to the next vowel. 반짝거리다 means the same; 반짝반짝 is the adverb.

T3-9163.forms: 번쩍 + 빛나다 / 들다 · 눈을 번쩍 뜨다 · 번쩍이다
T3-9163.m: with a flash; (lift) easily; (eyes) wide open
T3-9163.x: Lightning flashed, and then rain poured down.
T3-9163.e: Manner word (의태어) for a sudden bright flash, extended to anything sudden and easy. Bright-vowel 반짝 is a small, gentle glint.
T3-9163.t: 번쩍 들다 = to lift easily, 눈을 번쩍 뜨다 = eyes snap open, 정신이 번쩍 들다 = to come to one's senses. Verb: 번쩍이다.

T3-9164.x: The freshly made rice cake is still soft and squishy.
T3-9164.e: Manner word (의태어) for something soft and springy to the touch. Dark-vowel 물렁물렁 is softer and can sound mushy.
T3-9164.t: Usually as 말랑말랑하다; the short form 말랑하다 is also common.

T3-9165.x: I sharpened the pencil to a fine point.
T3-9165.t: Pronounced [뾰조카다]: ㄱ + ㅎ becomes ㅋ. 뾰족한 수가 없다 = 'there's no good way out'.

T3-9166.x: Grandpa, have you had your meal?
T3-9166.e: 잡수다 (itself an honorific of 먹다) + honorific -시-; the contracted 잡숫다 is also standard.
T3-9166.t: Pronounced [잡쑤시다]: the final ㅂ makes the next ㅅ tense. Use it for grandparents and the elderly; more deferential than 드시다.

T3-9167.forms: 여쭈워요 · 여쭈웠어요 · 여쭈울 거예요 (ㅂ irregular; humble, not used with -(으)세요)
T3-9167.ex: 교수님께 한 가지 여쭙고 싶은 게 있어요.
T3-9167.x: There's one thing I'd like to ask you, Professor.
T3-9167.e: Humble verb: it lowers the asker rather than raising the listener. 여쭈다 is an equally standard variant.
T3-9167.t: Pronounced [여쭙따]: the final ㅂ makes the next ㄷ tense. Use it with 께 when asking teachers, bosses or elders. In speech 여쭤보다 is most common.

T3-9168.x: Your son is already in college?
T3-9168.e: 아들 + honorific -님; the ㄹ drops before ㄴ, as in 따님.
T3-9168.t: Never use it for your own son; say 아들.

T3-9169.x: Your daughter looks a lot like you, ma'am.
T3-9169.e: 딸 + honorific -님; the ㄹ drops before ㄴ.
T3-9169.t: Never use it for your own daughter; say 딸.

T3-9170.m: COVID-19, the coronavirus; the COVID pandemic
T3-9170.ex: 코로나 때문에 이 년 동안 고향에 못 갔어요.
T3-9170.x: Because of COVID, I couldn't go back to my hometown for two years.
T3-9170.e: From 'corona(virus)'. The official Korean name is 코로나바이러스감염증-19, shortened to 코로나19 [코로나 일구].
T3-9170.t: Koreans say 코로나 for both the disease and the pandemic period: 코로나 때 'during COVID', 코로나에 걸리다 'to catch COVID'.

T3-9171.ex: 미세먼지가 심해서 공기 청정기를 계속 틀어 놨어요.
T3-9171.x: The fine dust is bad, so I've kept the air purifier running.
T3-9171.e: 空氣 'air' + 淸淨 'clean, pure' + 機 'machine'.
T3-9171.t: Turn it on with 켜다 or 틀다. A standard appliance in Korean homes because of 미세먼지 (fine dust). Also written 공기청정기.

T3-9172.x: I'll send you a message on KakaoTalk when I get home.
T3-9172.e: Short for 카카오톡 'KakaoTalk'; 톡 is from English 'talk'.
T3-9172.t: Casual. Almost everyone in Korea uses this messenger app, so 카톡 is used like 'text': 카톡해 'text me', 카톡 왔어요 'I got a message'.

T3-9173.x: I'll post the meeting place in the chat room.
T3-9173.t: Join or leave: 채팅방에 들어가다 / 채팅방을 나가다; invite someone: 채팅방에 초대하다. Casually also 톡방.

T3-9174.forms: 영상 통화가 · 영상 통화를 · verb: 영상 통화하다
T3-9174.ex: 주말마다 고향에 계신 부모님과 영상 통화를 해요.
T3-9174.x: Every weekend I have a video call with my parents back home.
T3-9174.e: 영상 'video, image' (literally 'reflected image') + 통화 'phone call' (literally 'talk passing through').
T3-9174.t: Make a video call: 영상 통화를 하다 or 영상 통화를 걸다. 화상 통화 means the same and is a slightly older, more formal term.

T3-9175.ex: 제 동생은 요리 유튜버가 되는 게 꿈이에요.
T3-9175.x: My younger sibling's dream is to become a cooking YouTuber.
T3-9175.t: Run a channel: 유튜브를 하다. A YouTuber with a big following is a 대형 유튜버, and one who deals with a topic is named after it: 먹방 유튜버, 여행 유튜버.

T3-9176.ex: 현금이 없으시면 계좌 이체로 보내 주셔도 돼요.
T3-9176.x: If you don't have cash, you can send it by bank transfer.
T3-9176.e: 계좌 'bank account' (literally 'counting place') + 이체 'transfer' (literally 'move and swap').
T3-9176.t: Transfers between Korean banks are fast and usually free in banking apps, so friends split bills and many small shops accept payment this way. Verb: 이체하다.

T3-9177.ex: 문자로 받은 인증 번호 여섯 자리를 입력하세요.
T3-9177.x: Enter the six-digit verification code you received by text.
T3-9177.t: Sign-ups and payments in Korea often need 휴대폰 인증 'phone verification': you get a code by text and must enter it within a few minutes.

T3-9178.x: Scan the QR code at the entrance and go in.
T3-9178.t: Read as 큐알 코드. 'Scan' is usually 찍다: QR 코드를 찍다. Many restaurants have a QR code on the table for the menu or ordering.

T3-9179.ex: 자취한 지 오래돼서 엄마가 해 준 집밥이 그리워요.
T3-9179.x: I've lived on my own for a long time, so I miss my mom's home cooking.
T3-9179.t: Pronounced [집빱]. It suggests warm, simple food with rice, soup and side dishes; restaurants advertise 집밥 같은 'just like home cooking'.

T3-9180.x: Today I joined a video conference from home.
T3-9180.e: 화상 'video image' (literally 'picture image') + 회의 'meeting' (literally 'meet and discuss').
T3-9180.t: Don't confuse this 화상 (畫像, image) with its homonym 화상 (火傷) 'burn'. 회의 is usually pronounced [회이].

T3-9181.forms: casual exclamation · 헐, 대박! · 헐, 진짜?
T3-9181.m: what?!, OMG, no way (shock or disbelief)
T3-9181.x: What?! The tickets are already sold out?
T3-9181.e: A stunned sound word that spread through internet chat in the 2000s and moved into everyday speech.
T3-9181.t: Casual: fine with friends, not with bosses or elders. It can greet good or bad news but usually carries dismay or disbelief.

T3-9182.forms: 짱이에요 · 짱이다 · 짱 + adjective (짱 좋아요 = super good)
T3-9182.m: the best, awesome; super, really (before adjectives)
T3-9182.x: The tteokbokki here is seriously the best!
T3-9182.e: Often linked to 장 (長) 'head, chief', said with a tense consonant for emphasis; the origin is not certain.
T3-9182.t: Casual. A thumbs-up with 짱! means 'the best!'. Also found in compounds like 얼짱 'great-looking (literally face-best)'.

T3-9183.m: gasp!, yikes, oh no (sudden surprise or shock)
T3-9183.x: Yikes, I left my wallet at home!
T3-9183.e: A sound word imitating a sharp intake of breath. Doubled, 헉헉 imitates panting.
T3-9183.t: Casual and very common in texts. 헉 is a quick startled reaction; 헐 is more stunned disbelief.

T3-9184.forms: 세상에! · stronger: 세상에나! · 세상에, 이럴 수가!
T3-9184.m: oh my God!, good heavens!, my goodness
T3-9184.ex: 세상에, 이 많은 음식을 혼자 다 만들었어요?
T3-9184.x: Good heavens, you made all this food by yourself?
T3-9184.e: 세상 'the world' (literally 'upon the world') + 에 'in' — as if saying 'in all the world, how can this be?'
T3-9184.t: Shows amazement or shock, good or bad. 세상에나 is stronger and sounds a bit older or more motherly.

T3-9185.forms: casual reply · polite: 그러게요 · 그러게 말이야 (strong agreement)
T3-9185.m: I know, right; tell me about it; yeah (casual agreement)
T3-9185.x: I know, right? It's really hot today.
T3-9185.e: From 그렇다 'to be so' + -게, used as a reply: 'it is so, indeed'.
T3-9185.t: Casual 반말 for friends; add 요 to be polite. In another tone, 그러게 내가 뭐랬어 means 'See, what did I tell you?'

T3-9186.forms: 에이! · 에이, 설마 · 에이, 아니에요 (modest denial)
T3-9186.m: come on, no way, aw (doubt, dismissal or mild disappointment)
T3-9186.x: Oh, come on, is that really true?
T3-9186.e: An interjection of doubt or mild letdown, close to English 'aw, come on'.
T3-9186.t: Also brushes off praise modestly: 에이, 아니에요 'Oh no, not at all.' Stretched 에이~ sounds teasing.

T3-9187.m: ugh, phew, sigh (frustration, tiredness or relief)
T3-9187.ex: 어휴, 오늘 일이 왜 이렇게 많아요?
T3-9187.x: Ugh, why is there so much work today?
T3-9187.e: Imitates a long sigh. 휴 alone is more often a sigh of relief.
T3-9187.t: Mostly shows frustration or exhaustion, so it can sound like complaining; be careful in front of superiors.

T3-9188.x: On the weekend I recharged by walking a forest trail.
T3-9188.e: From English 'healing'. In Korean it means relaxing and recovering from stress, not medical healing.
T3-9188.t: Very common: 힐링 여행 'relaxing trip', 힐링이 돼요 'It's so soothing'.

T3-9189.x: If you order in the morning, it's delivered the same day.
T3-9189.e: 당일 'the very day' + 배송 'delivery' (literally 'distribute and send').
T3-9189.t: Compare 익일 배송 'next-day delivery' and 새벽 배송 'early-morning delivery'.

T3-9190.m: secondhand trading, buying and selling used goods
T3-9190.ex: 안 쓰는 물건은 중고 거래로 팔아요.
T3-9190.x: I sell things I don't use through secondhand trading.
T3-9190.t: Mostly done on neighborhood apps, often as 직거래 (meeting in person); watch out for 사기 (scams) when paying in advance.

T3-9191.x: These days you order at a kiosk even in restaurants.
T3-9191.e: From English 'kiosk'; in Korea it almost always means a touchscreen machine for ordering and paying, not a street stall.
T3-9191.t: Common in fast-food places and cafés. Many older people find them hard to use, so some shops keep a staffed counter too.

T3-9192.forms: N뿐이에요 · N뿐(만) 아니라 (not only N) · after verbs: -(으)ㄹ 뿐이에요
T3-9192.ex: 우리 반에서 안경 쓴 사람은 저뿐이에요.
T3-9192.x: I'm the only one in our class who wears glasses.
T3-9192.e: Native word. After a noun it's a particle (저뿐); after a verb it's a bound noun written with a space (웃을 뿐이에요).
T3-9192.t: 뿐 is almost always followed by 이다 or 아니라: 저뿐이에요 'it's only me'; 한국어뿐만 아니라 영어도 'not only Korean but also English'.

T3-9193.forms: 이라도 after a consonant (물이라도) · 라도 after a vowel (커피라도) · 누구라도, 언제라도 (any-)
T3-9193.m: even if it's just, at least (second-best choice); any- (누구라도 anyone)
T3-9193.x: If you're hungry, do you want to eat at least some ramyeon?
T3-9193.e: From 이다 'to be' + -라도 'even if' — 'even if it is (only) X'.
T3-9193.t: Shows X isn't ideal but will do. It softens offers and suggestions: 차라도 한잔할까요? 'Shall we at least have some tea?'

T3-9194.forms: 이든지 after a consonant (무엇이든지) · 든지 after a vowel (누구든지) · short form: (이)든
T3-9194.x: If you have any questions, ask me anytime.
T3-9194.t: With question words it means 'any-': 누구든지 'anyone', 뭐든지 'anything', 어디든지 'anywhere'. In speech it's often shortened: 뭐든 괜찮아요.

T3-9195.forms: Same form after any noun: 형만큼 · 이만큼 · N만큼 …지 않다 (not as … as N)
T3-9195.x: Seoul wasn't as cold as I thought.
T3-9195.e: Native word. After verbs it's a bound noun written with a space: 먹을 만큼 'as much as you'll eat'.
T3-9195.t: 노력한 만큼 결과가 나와요 'You get results in proportion to your effort' — a very common use after verbs.

T3-9196.forms: Same form after any noun: 계획대로 · 약속대로 · 순서대로
T3-9196.m: according to, as (it is), just like
T3-9196.e: Native word. After verbs it's a bound noun written with a space: 말한 대로 'as I said'.
T3-9196.t: Handy set phrases: 마음대로 'as you like', 순서대로 'in order', 사실대로 'truthfully'.

T3-9197.forms: N 말고 N: 이거 말고 저거 · 커피 말고 차 · N 말고도 (besides N)
T3-9197.m: not … but, instead of; other than, besides
T3-9197.x: Do you have any other colors besides this one?
T3-9197.e: From the verb 말다 'to stop, not do' + -고: 'leaving X aside'.
T3-9197.t: Very common when shopping or ordering: 이거 말고 저거 주세요. 말고도 means 'besides': 저 말고도 올 사람이 많아요 'Lots of people are coming besides me.'

T3-9198.forms: N에 비해(서) · N에 비하면 · -는 것에 비해
T3-9198.ex: 이 식당은 가격에 비해 양이 많아요.
T3-9198.x: This restaurant gives big portions for the price.
T3-9198.t: Often means 'for' in judgments: 나이에 비해 어려 보여요 'You look young for your age.'

T3-9199.forms: 과 달리 after a consonant (예상과 달리) · 와 달리 after a vowel (어제와 달리)
T3-9199.x: Unlike yesterday, the weather is clear today.
T3-9199.t: 예상과 달리 'contrary to expectations' is a common set phrase. In conversation 하고 달리 or (이)랑 달리 also work.

T3-9200.forms: A. 그러니 B. (B is often a suggestion or command) · more common in speech: 그러니까
T3-9200.ex: 내일 비가 온대요. 그러니 우산 꼭 챙기세요.
T3-9200.x: They say it'll rain tomorrow. So be sure to take an umbrella.
T3-9200.e: 그렇다 'to be so' + -(으)니 'since': 'since it is so'.
T3-9200.t: A shorter, slightly more written form of 그러니까. Like 그러니까 — and unlike 그래서 — it can be followed by commands and suggestions.

T3-9201.forms: A. 그렇다고 B. (B usually negative) · fuller form: 그렇다고 해서
T3-9201.m: but that doesn't mean, even so
T3-9201.ex: 일이 많긴 해요. 그렇다고 그만둘 수는 없잖아요.
T3-9201.x: I do have a lot of work. But that doesn't mean I can quit, right?
T3-9201.e: 그렇다 'to be so' + -다고 (quoting): 'just because it is so …'.
T3-9201.t: Pronounced [그러타고]. The next sentence denies the conclusion you might expect: 그렇다고 포기하면 안 돼요 'But that's no reason to give up.'

T3-9202.forms: A. 그렇지 않으면 B. · casual: 안 그러면
T3-9202.ex: 빨리 출발해요. 그렇지 않으면 길이 막혀요.
T3-9202.x: Let's leave quickly. Otherwise we'll hit traffic.
T3-9202.e: 그렇다 'to be so' + -지 않으면 'if not': 'if it isn't so'.
T3-9202.t: Pronounced [그러치 아느면]. In casual speech people usually say 안 그러면: 서둘러, 안 그러면 늦어.

T3-9203.forms: A. 그 대신 B. · N 대신 (instead of N)
T3-9203.ex: 제가 밥을 살게요. 그 대신 커피는 사 주세요.
T3-9203.x: I'll buy the meal. In return, you get the coffee.
T3-9203.t: Often introduces a trade-off or condition: 싸요. 그 대신 좀 멀어요 'It's cheap, but on the other hand it's a bit far.'

T3-9204.forms: 도대체 + question word: 도대체 왜 · 도대체 뭐 · 도대체 어디 · short: 대체
T3-9204.m: on earth, in the world (what/why on earth …?)
T3-9204.x: Why on earth didn't you answer the phone?
T3-9204.e: Originally 'on the whole, in general' (all + general outline); now used to stress a question.
T3-9204.t: Shows frustration or strong curiosity. In casual speech it's often shortened to 대체: 대체 왜?

T3-9205.forms: 마침 + clause: 마침 잘됐다 (perfect timing) · 마침 그때
T3-9205.m: just then, just in time, conveniently, as it happens
T3-9205.ex: 마침 잘 오셨어요. 지금 전화하려고 했어요.
T3-9205.x: You came at just the right time. I was about to call you.
T3-9205.e: Native adverb: things happen to fit at the right moment. Different from 마침내 'finally'.
T3-9205.t: Usually for good timing: 마침 잘됐네요! 'Perfect timing!' For bad timing, Koreans say 하필.

T3-9206.m: how should I put it, sort of
T3-9206.x: That movie was, how should I put it, kind of strange.
T3-9206.e: Contraction of 뭐라고 할까 'what shall I call it'.
T3-9206.t: Buys time while you look for the right word; common in casual talk and interviews.

T3-9207.m: come to think of it, now that you mention it
T3-9207.x: Come to think of it, today is Mom's birthday!
T3-9207.e: 그러다 'to do so' + -고 보니 'having done it, (I realize)'.
T3-9207.t: Used when something said or seen suddenly reminds you of something. It often goes with the 'discovery' ending -네요.

T3-9208.ex: 그 회사는 작년에 매출이 1조 원을 넘었어요.
T3-9208.x: That company's sales passed one trillion won last year.
T3-9208.e: The next big unit after 억: 10,000억 = 1조.
T3-9208.t: Korean counts big numbers in groups of four zeros: 만 (10⁴), 억 (10⁸), 조 (10¹²). Don't confuse it with 조 (組) 'group, team', as in 조별 과제.

T3-9209.forms: 수십 명 · 수십 개 · 수십 번 · 수십만
T3-9209.ex: 식당 앞에 사람들이 수십 명 줄을 서 있었어요.
T3-9209.x: Dozens of people were lined up in front of the restaurant.
T3-9209.t: 수 + a number unit means 'several …': 수십, 수백, 수천, 수만. It is never an exact figure.

T3-9210.ex: 그 영상에 하루 만에 댓글이 수백 개 달렸어요.
T3-9210.x: That video got hundreds of comments in a single day.
T3-9210.t: Combine with 만 for bigger amounts: 수백만 명 'millions of people'.

T3-9211.x: Thousands of people gathered at the weekend festival.
T3-9211.t: For tens of thousands, Korean uses 수만 ('several 만'), not '수십 천'.

T3-9212.x: This cup holds 300 milliliters of water.
T3-9212.t: In everyday speech people often shorten it to 미리: 오백 미리 생수 'a 500 ml bottle of water'.

T3-9213.ex: 이 트럭에는 짐을 5톤까지 실을 수 있어요.
T3-9213.x: This truck can carry up to 5 tons of cargo.
T3-9213.e: From English 'ton'; in Korea it means the metric ton, 1,000 kg.
T3-9213.t: A separate loanword 톤 means 'tone': 목소리 톤 'tone of voice', 피부 톤 'skin tone'.
